description: 3D printing, metal sintering and SLA — what each does and when to use it.
content_html:
What Is Additive Manufacturing?

Additive manufacturing is the opposite of cutting or drilling: instead of removing material, you build a part up, one thin layer at a time. A digital 3D model (usually saved as an STL file) is sliced into hundreds of horizontal layers by software, and the machine deposits or fuses material along each slice until the full shape is complete. Because no specialist tooling — moulds, dies, jigs — is required, a new design can go from computer screen to physical object in hours rather than weeks.

Key Fact

Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from a digital model (STL file). No moulds or dies are needed, so tooling cost is effectively zero for a one-off part.

Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)

Fused deposition modelling (FDM) is the most common form of 3D printing found in schools and small workshops. A spool of thermoplastic filament — typically PLA or ABS — is fed into a heated nozzle. The nozzle melts the plastic and extrudes it in precise paths across the build platform. Each layer bonds to the one below as it cools, and the platform drops slightly before the next layer is deposited. A support structure is printed under overhanging sections and removed afterwards.

FDM is ideal for concept models, ergonomic prototypes and functional parts that do not need very smooth surfaces. Typical layer thickness is 0.1–0.3 mm. The main limitations are visible layer lines on the surface and relatively low mechanical strength compared with injection-moulded parts. Consumer FDM printers such as the Bambu Lab range have made this technology genuinely accessible at under £300.

Stereolithography (SLA) cures liquid photopolymer resin with an ultraviolet laser. The build platform starts just below the surface of the resin vat; the laser traces each layer, hardening only the areas it touches. The platform then drops by one layer thickness and the next cross-section is cured. SLA produces parts with an extremely smooth surface finish and fine detail, making it popular for jewellery, dental models and appearance prototypes in product design studios. Resin is more expensive than FDM filament and uncured resin requires careful handling as a chemical irritant.

Rapid prototyping using SLA is particularly valued when a design team needs a high-fidelity model to present to a client before committing to expensive injection-mould tooling. Dyson engineers, for example, use SLA models to evaluate cyclone geometry before the tooling investment is made.

Metal Sintering

Metal sintering (also called selective laser sintering or SLS when applied to metals, or DMLS — Direct Metal Laser Sintering) spreads a thin layer of metal powder across the build platform and a laser selectively fuses the particles. Unfused powder acts as its own support structure and is recycled after the build. The result is a fully dense metal component with mechanical properties close to those of a traditionally machined part.

Metal sintering is used across aerospace, automotive and medical engineering for parts that are geometrically too complex to machine conventionally — internal cooling channels inside a turbine blade, for instance, or a lightweight titanium bracket for an aircraft seat with internal lattice structures. Rolls-Royce uses metal sintering for low-volume turbine components. The process is slow and the machines cost hundreds of thousands of pounds, so it is reserved for high-value, low-volume parts.

Key Fact

FDM (thermoplastic filament), SLA (UV-cured resin) and metal sintering (laser-fused powder) are three distinct additive routes. FDM is cheapest; SLA gives the best surface finish; metal sintering produces functional metal parts with complex geometry.

Additive Manufacturing vs Mass Production

A common error is to describe additive manufacturing as a mass-production method. It is not. The table below captures the key differences examiners reward.

Tooling cost: Additive manufacturing requires no moulds, dies or fixtures — the digital model is sent straight to the machine. Injection moulding, by contrast, requires a steel mould that can cost £20,000–£200,000 before a single part is made. Additive manufacturing therefore has zero tooling cost, making one-off and low-volume production economically viable.

Speed of iteration: A designer can update a CAD model and have a revised prototype in hand within hours. With traditional tooling, modifying a mould takes days or weeks and costs thousands of pounds. This is why product development teams use additive manufacturing for rapid prototyping during the design iteration phase.

Geometric freedom: Additive processes can produce internal cavities, lattice structures and undercuts that are impossible or prohibitively expensive to machine. Conventional subtractive machining is limited by tool access; additive is limited only by the digital model.

Production volume: Additive manufacturing is slow per part. A single FDM print of a mobile phone case takes 2–4 hours. Injection moulding cycles in 30–60 seconds. For volumes above a few thousand units, injection moulding almost always has a lower unit cost once the tooling cost is amortised.

Material waste: Additive manufacturing adds material only where needed — waste is minimal. Subtractive processes (milling, turning) can waste 90% of the starting billet for complex aerospace parts. This makes additive manufacturing more sustainable for expensive materials such as titanium.

Rapid Prototyping in the Engineering Design Process

Rapid prototyping sits between the design phase and the production phase. An engineer creates a CAD model, exports it as an STL file, and feeds it to an additive manufacturing machine. The resulting prototype is used to test fit, form and function before committing to expensive tooling. This compresses the design cycle significantly: Tesla’s Gigafactory uses additive manufacturing to iterate on manufacturing jigs and tooling fixtures at speed, avoiding the lead times of conventional fabrication. Once the design is finalised, mass production typically uses a different process — injection moulding, die casting or CNC machining — better suited to high volumes.
exam_tip_html: When an exam question asks you to explain advantages of additive manufacturing, do not just write “fast” or “cheap” — these alone score no marks. Explain WHY it is fast or cost-effective for this situation: “no tooling is required, so a one-off prototype can be made without the cost of a mould” scores the mark. Equally, if asked to compare additive manufacturing with mass production, make the distinction explicit — additive suits low-volume, high-complexity, short-lead-time work; mass production (injection moulding, die casting) suits high-volume once tooling cost is spread across thousands of parts.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from a digital model (STL file) — FDM extrudes thermoplastic, SLA cures resin with UV light, and metal sintering fuses metal powder with a laser.
  • Rapid prototyping uses additive manufacturing to test a design quickly and cheaply before expensive tooling is committed — it is NOT a mass-production method.
  • Key advantages are zero tooling cost, fast design iteration and geometric freedom; key limitation is slow build speed making it uneconomical for large production volumes.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes fused deposition modelling (FDM)?
A) A laser cures liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer
B) A laser fuses metal powder layer by layer
C) A heated nozzle extrudes melted thermoplastic filament layer by layer
D) A router cuts a 3D shape from a solid block of plastic
practice_questions.marks: C) A heated nozzle extrudes melted thermoplastic filament layer by layer [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the file format used to transfer a 3D CAD model to an additive manufacturing machine.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Name a Material or Process
practice_questions.marks: STL (Standard Tessellation Language / stereolithography file) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why an engineer might choose additive manufacturing rather than injection moulding to produce a prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any two of:
- No tooling (mould) required, so there is no tooling cost for a one-off part
- Design can be changed quickly in CAD and re-printed, allowing rapid iteration
- Can produce complex internal geometries or undercuts that moulding cannot
- Short lead time — a prototype can be ready in hours rather than weeks
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stages involved in producing a part using fused deposition modelling (FDM).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any four of the following stages in a logical order:
1. Create or obtain a 3D CAD model of the part
2. Export/save the model as an STL file
3. Import the STL file into slicing software; set layer thickness and generate support structures
4. The heated nozzle melts thermoplastic filament and extrudes it onto the build platform
5. Each layer bonds to the one below as it cools; the platform lowers by one layer thickness
6. The process repeats until the part is complete; support material is removed
[4 marks — 1 mark per valid stage, must be in a logical manufacturing order]

practice_questions.text:
Holbrook Designs Ltd is a product design studio developing a new ergonomic handle for a power tool. The studio needs three prototypes to present to the client next week. The final product will be injection moulded in ABS in quantities of 50,000 units per year.

Evaluate whether additive manufacturing is a suitable choice for producing the three prototypes. In your answer, consider the advantages and limitations of additive manufacturing for this situation compared with other available methods.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Clear evaluation of both additive manufacturing and at least one alternative, with advantages and limitations linked explicitly to the details of the scenario (3 prototypes, one-week deadline, eventual high-volume injection moulding). A justified conclusion about whether additive manufacturing is suitable.

Secure (5-6 marks): Advantages and limitations both addressed with some link to the scenario. Some comparison made. Conclusion present but may be underdeveloped.

Developing (3-4 marks): Advantages or limitations covered but not both. Limited link to scenario specifics. Conclusion weak or absent.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Generic points about 3D printing with little or no reference to the scenario.

Content that may be credited:
Advantages for this scenario: no tooling cost for 3 units; STL file can be printed within the one-week deadline; design iteration is possible if changes arise; complex ergonomic geometry (curves, grip features) is achievable.
Limitations: surface finish may show layer lines (may not matter for internal client presentation but matters if the prototype is for a consumer show); material properties of FDM ABS differ from injection-moulded ABS; printing 3 units still takes several hours each.
Alternative: hand-carved foam or machined model — slower and less accurate for ergonomic geometry.
Conclusion: additive manufacturing (FDM or SLA) is well suited for this low-volume rapid prototyping task, but the studio should note that the final product will require injection moulding tooling investment before volume production.

practice_questions.text: Compare stereolithography (SLA) and metal sintering as additive manufacturing processes. In your answer, refer to the materials used, the energy source, the surface finish achieved and a typical application for each.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for developed comparative points. Up to 6 marks across the four areas:

Materials: SLA uses liquid photopolymer resin; metal sintering uses fine metal powder (e.g. stainless steel, titanium, aluminium alloy).

Energy source: SLA uses an ultraviolet laser to cure/harden the resin; metal sintering uses a high-powered infrared laser to fuse the powder particles.

Surface finish: SLA produces a very smooth surface finish with fine detail, better than FDM; metal sintering produces a slightly rough surface (powder granules) but close to the finish of machined metal.

Typical application: SLA — appearance prototypes, dental models, jewellery; metal sintering — aerospace turbine components, medical implants, lightweight structural brackets.

[6 marks — must compare, not just describe each in isolation. 1 mark per simple point, 2 marks for a developed comparative point. Max 6.]

knowledge_checks.q: Which additive manufacturing process uses a UV laser to cure liquid photopolymer resin?
Why does additive manufacturing have a very low tooling cost for one-off parts?
options: The machine runs at very low temperatures
The materials used are inexpensive polymers
No moulds, dies or fixtures are needed — only a digital model
The process is fully automated with no operator needed

knowledge_checks.q: A 3D CAD model is exported as an _____ file before it is sent to an additive manufacturing machine.
Metal sintering uses a high-powered laser to fuse fine _____ particles together layer by layer.
Match each additive manufacturing process to its key feature:
right: Extrudes melted thermoplastic filament through a heated nozzle
Cures liquid resin with a UV laser for smooth surface finish
Fuses metal powder with a laser to produce dense metal parts

flashcard_questions.q: What does additive manufacturing build from?
flashcard_questions.a: A digital 3D model (STL file), adding material layer by layer.

flashcard_questions.q: What thermoplastics are typically used in FDM 3D printing?
flashcard_questions.a: PLA and ABS are the most common.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of slicing software in additive manufacturing?
flashcard_questions.a: It divides the 3D model into thin horizontal layers for the machine to follow.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of material does SLA (stereolithography) use?
flashcard_questions.a: Liquid photopolymer resin, hardened by a UV laser.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does SLA produce a better surface finish than FDM?
flashcard_questions.a: UV-cured resin resolves finer detail and has no visible filament layer lines.

flashcard_questions.q: What is metal sintering used for in aerospace engineering?
flashcard_questions.a: Complex metal parts such as turbine components with internal cooling channels.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is additive manufacturing NOT used for mass production?
flashcard_questions.a: It is slow per part; injection moulding is faster and cheaper at high volumes.
Using additive manufacturing to make a test model quickly before final tooling is committed.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one advantage of additive manufacturing for low-volume production.
flashcard_questions.a: No tooling (moulds or dies) required, so there is no tooling cost for a one-off.

flashcard_questions.q: What geometric feature can additive manufacturing produce that CNC machining cannot?
flashcard_questions.a: Internal cavities and lattice structures unreachable by a cutting tool.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the STL file format stand for?
flashcard_questions.a: Standard Tessellation Language (also Standard Triangulation Language).

flashcard_questions.q: Which additive process is most likely to be found in a school workshop?
flashcard_questions.a: Fused deposition modelling (FDM) — low cost and uses safe thermoplastic filament.

glossary_terms.definition: A manufacturing method that builds up a part layer by layer from a digital model, adding material only where needed.
An additive process that melts a thermoplastic filament and extrudes it through a heated nozzle onto a build platform, building the part layer by layer.
An additive process that uses an ultraviolet laser to cure (harden) a liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer inside a vat.
An additive process that uses a high-powered laser to fuse fine metal powder particles together layer by layer, producing fully dense metal parts.
